 Born in Corduba, modern-day Córdoba, Spain, and raised in Rome, he became one of the most influential thinkers of the ancient world. 

He served as an advisor and tutor to Emperor Nero, but his true legacy came from his writings on self-control, suffering, wealth, death, anger, and the discipline of the mind.

Seneca believed that life was not made easier by avoiding hardship, but by learning how to endure it with dignity. His philosophy taught that a person should not be ruled by fear, pleasure, anger, or the opinions of others. To him, real power came from mastering yourself, accepting what you cannot control, and living with virtue even when life becomes painful or unfair.

In 65 CE, Seneca was ordered by Nero to take his own life after being accused of involvement in a conspiracy. He faced death in the same spirit he wrote about: calmly, deliberately, and with philosophical strength. Nearly 2,000 years later, his words still speak to anyone trying to stay composed in chaos, suffer without breaking, and become stronger through discipline.

The Beauty Standard Hidden In Medieval Portraits

“Now I understand why people can spend hours looking at the same painting.”

Once you notice it, you start seeing it everywhere. In portraits by Jan van Eyck, Rogier van der Weyden, Hans Memling, Petrus Christus, and other artists of the 15th century, many women are painted with unusually high, exposed foreheads.

It was not a mistake. In late medieval and early Renaissance Europe, a high forehead could be seen as a sign of beauty, intelligence, refinement, and noble status. Women who did not naturally have the look could pluck their hairlines, remove brows, or wear headpieces that made the forehead appear even taller.

That is why portraits like “Portrait of a Lady”, “Maria Portinari”, “Portrait of a Young Girl”, and even the women painted by Jan van Eyck can look strange to modern eyes. These faces were not simply being recorded. They were also being shaped by the beauty standards of their time.

The detail makes these paintings feel more human. Behind the perfect stillness of medieval portraits were people living inside trends, expectations, status symbols, and pressures that feel surprisingly familiar. The high forehead may look unusual now, but in their world, it was elegance, wealth, and beauty written directly onto the face.

Dbt89BggZd9.caption:
The Jim CARREY Paintings You Don’t Know About
By Jim Carrey

“Now I understand why people can spend hours looking at the same painting.”

Most people know Jim Carrey as the actor behind films like The Mask, Ace Ventura, and The Truman Show. But away from acting, he has been drawing since childhood and began painting obsessively around 2011 while trying to heal a broken heart. During a bleak New York winter, he filled his home with enormous canvases because, as he later explained, he “needed color.”

His studio became so crowded that he could barely move through it. Carrey paints with brushes, pours paint directly onto canvases, works with his hands, and sometimes scrapes away entire sections before rebuilding them. In the 2017 short documentary ‘I Needed Color’, he described art as a physical model of an artist’s inner life. The darkness in his paintings reveals what he has lived through, while their brightness reveals what he is still reaching toward.

Many of the works are intensely personal and spiritual. ‘Electric Jesus’ transforms Christ into a blazing field of color, with eyes intended to communicate complete acceptance and forgiveness. ‘Sunshower’ uses simultaneous rain and sunlight as a symbol of pain cleansing the way toward renewed appreciation for life. In ‘Hooray We Are All Broken’, fragmented figures dance together while believing they are separate, even though they share the same energy.

Carrey’s first solo exhibition, ‘Nothing to See Here’, featured around 40 works in 2011, followed by more than 60 paintings and sculptures in ‘Sunshower’ in 2017. He later turned his restless line toward political cartoons, using grotesque humor and anger to confront contemporary American politics. His visual art feels like the private opposite of his acting: instead of transforming himself into characters for an audience, he uses color to reveal what remains when the performance ends.
